en: The Ritual Manual for the Successive Stages of the Maṇḍala Practice of the Eight-Syllable Secret Dhāraṇī of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, in One Scroll;
excerpted from the *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-samāja-sūtra*, from the Chapter on the Elimination of Calamities, Rescue from Perils, and the Pacification of Obstacles.

Translated by the śramaṇa Bodhiliśi of the Great Nālandā Monastery in Central India, who was pure in his observance of the precepts; personally received from the pen of [the master] and transmitted by the monk Yiyun. The name of this Tripiṭaka master in the land of Han is Bodhisena. At that time, the World-Honored One...
He addressed Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, saying:
"This place where the eight-syllable supreme mantra of great majestic power resides is no different from the Buddha being present in person."
It can manifest the various inconceivable supernatural powers of all Buddhas and can also perform great,
immeasurable transformations of spiritual penetrations.
I shall now briefly praise a small portion of the merits of this dhāraṇī.
If I were to explain it in full detail,
even in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great eons, I could not finish speaking.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
He then spoke the eight-syllable heart-mantra of Mahātejas:
Oṃ āḥ vīra hūṃ kha ca la. He further addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Lord:
Regarding this dharani:
if there are men or women who are unable to perform the rites of service and offering, or who,
being laypeople, are constrained by their various worldly occupations;
Provided that one can maintain it in memory without forgetting and recite it at the proper times,
and perform offerings according to one's means without omission— even if only a small portion—
one will achieve accomplishment by providing whatever one is personally able to do.
Except for those who lack a sincere mind or right faith,
who do not resolve to attain the Mahāyāna bodhicitta,
and who engage in slandering the Triple Gem.
If one gives rise to unwholesome conduct and various evil karmas,
even the smallest of dharmas cannot be accomplished by such a mind;
how much less could a great dharma be accomplished?
At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, saying:
"If there are good men or good women..."
If one can recite this dhāraṇī once, one immediately attains self-protection;
if one recites it twice, one can protect one's companions;
if one recites it three times, one will greatly protect one's dwelling place.
Even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages cannot surpass it,
let alone lesser beings. If one recites it four times,
one will immediately obtain protection for one's wife and children.
If one recites it five times, one will be able to protect all of one's kinsmen and retinues.
If one recites it six times, one will be able to protect all cities, towns, villages, hamlets, and so forth.
If one recites it seven times, one will be able to protect all sentient beings from various sufferings and hardships.
When about to put on one's clothes, one should empower them by reciting it seven times;
this can eliminate all evil poisons and various calamities.
When washing one's hands or face,
empower pure water seven times and then wash the hands and face;
this will cause sentient beings to hold one in high esteem and reverence.
All those with evil views shall be completely subdued;
all people shall bow before them with reverence and respect,
causing their evil minds to be eliminated and hearts of joy to arise.
If a person suffers from pain in the body or its limbs and joints,
they should empower warm water one hundred and eight times and bathe with it;
they will immediately have auspicious dreams and attain recovery.
If, every morning at dawn,
one takes a handful of water, empowers it seven times with mantras,
and drinks it into the body;
All retributions for evil deeds shall be completely extinguished;
how much more so for those who are free from calamities.
Furthermore, the defilements of the three karmas shall also be washed away, and one’s lifespan shall be long and enduring.
If one consecrates food and drink seven times with this mantra,
even poison will be unable to harm those who eat it.
If one encounters wicked people or enemies...
One should perform recitation;
thus, one will naturally subdue oneself, eliminate and restrain the mind of anger, and turn toward others with a heart of loving-kindness.
If there is a place of fear, one should recite with utmost sincerity.
One will immediately attain fearlessness.
If one recites it one hundred and eight times while lying down,
one will immediately obtain auspicious dreams through which one can discern matters of good and evil.
If a person suffers from malaria,
the reciter should gaze at the face of that afflicted person and recite this mantra one thousand and eight times.
The malarial fever shall be immediately cured.
When entering into battle,
one should write this mantra with ox-gallstone and wear it upon the body.
No swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, or axes shall be able to harm them.
When entering into battle,
one should draw an image of the youth Mañjuśrī along with his mantra.
Placing the elephant upon a horse, it shall lead the way at the front of the army;
neither the various troops nor the enemies will be able to cause harm,
and they will naturally retreat and disperse.
One must constantly recite it;
all transgressions, including the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the ten evil deeds, will be completely extinguished,
and one shall behold Mañjuśrī face to face.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one must always receive, uphold, recite, and maintain this in mind without forgetting.
Recite it one hundred and eight times each time, never allowing the practice to be interrupted;
thus, one will always bring all sentient beings under subjugation.
If one empowers the topknot seven times,
all sentient beings who see it shall subdue evil persons, causing them to retreat and disperse.
If one can enter the maṇḍala according to the ritual three times each day,
reciting it one hundred and eight times for each session;
All that is sought shall be obtained as desired, perfectly fulfilled;
one will attain great wealth and nobility, with mastery over all actions.
At the time of death, one will attain the Samantamukha Samādhi.
Upon seeing Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
the World-Honored One then addressed the great assembly once more.
O Bodhisattvas,
I shall now further explain the sequential ritual for the maṇḍala altar of the eight-syllable mantra of supreme and great majestic power.
You should listen attentively.
If one wishes to establish a śāntika maṇḍala,
one should first select the site;
it must be located within a pure monastery.
Either in a mountain deep forest at a most auspicious and supreme site,
or in a city, town, or village at a superior and meritorious location where flowers,
fruits, and milky trees grow in abundance.
Establishing a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs of profound practice,
as well as for sons and daughters of good family.
Generating a heart of compassionate resolve,
one constructs a maṇḍala and performs the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra,
vowing to rescue and protect sentient beings during times of urgent distress.
One who wishes to receive and uphold this mantra should first seek out a virtuous Great Ācārya who understands the true path and its practice, and receive empowerment from him.
Having received the empowerment, [one should proceed].
I respectfully submit this request for the transmission and reception of this teaching.
Only after having personally received the transmission may one practice its recitation.
This is especially so in cases of urgent distress or fearful circumstances.
One should prepare a maṇḍala by grinding fragrant unguents upon an open space; there,
one should merely inscribe the mantra and seed-syllables,
while visualizing the form and color of the deity.
One should perform the appropriate rites of empowerment, recitation, and protection.
If one intends to draw a mandala out of pride,
one must not use leather glue.
One should use pure fragrant liquid to mix the colors for painting.
If one intends to perform long-term recitation,
one should then dig the ground according to the ritual rules.
Separately select earth from the riverbank that is firm, excellent, sweet and light in taste, white, moist, fine-textured, and slightly yellowish-red.
Having obtained it, mix it with scented water and construct the altar.
Perform the consecration according to the sequence of the instructions.
The artisans must bathe daily in pure water, don new and clean garments,
and only after having received the eightfold precepts (aṣṭāṅga-śīla) may they begin their work.
The methods within the remaining *siddhi*-reliances cannot be explained in full detail.
Regarding the method for the maṇḍala:
first, one should mentally create a circular wheel like the full moon.
In the center, write the full syllable *maṃ* in Brahmī script.
Next, from behind the syllable, write the syllable *oṃ* facing north. Then, proceeding clockwise, write the long-syllabled *ā* at the northeast corner, with the sound of the syllable *e*.
Next, in the east, write the long vowel *ras* (味).
Next, in the southeast corner, write the syllable *ra* (羅).
Next, in the south, write the long vowel *hūṃ* (𤙖).
Next, write the syllable *kha* (􄑌) at the southwest corner.
Next, write the syllable *za* (􄑼) in the west.
Next, write the syllable *la* (􄙉) at the northwest corner.
These nine syllables constitute the central deity within the inner court.
Alternatively, one may paint the youth Mañjuśrī within the court, with eight topknots on his head:
five front topknots, one topknot at the crown, and two topknots at the back, each with a single tuft of hair upon it.
All possess the Buddha-body; this is called the method of painted images.
If one seeks blessings, prosperity, rank, position, or auspicious matters, one should write the syllable Śrī within the heart [of the image].
If one seeks to pacify calamities, eliminate difficulties, and utterly extinguish the seven kinds of disasters—
namely, eclipses of the sun and moon, the five planets deviating from their regular courses, and the concurrent uprising of armies and bandits— then [one should practice].
Floods and droughts occur out of season;
wind and rain fall in violation of their proper measure;
and wicked ministers act in rebellion, bringing harm to the people.
Wild beasts and evil creatures devour sentient beings;
the five grains do not flourish.
Such calamities and urgent perils as official reprimands, royal troubles, the danger of death, and various forms of fear shall [be averted].
If one wishes to cause [afflictions] to dissipate,
one should write the syllable *Pam* (𑖥) in the heart.
If one seeks to subjugate an enemy so that they abandon their evil intentions and become well-disposed, [one should do the same].
In the center, write the character "Dàn" (淡).
If there are evil persons who are difficult to subdue—
such as butchers, hunters, or non-Buddhists who do not believe in the Buddha-dharma— [then this is to be applied].
To cause malevolent minds to be crushed and destroyed, or to cause them to be shattered,
one should write the Sanskrit syllable *ṣṭrīḥ* within the heart;
this concludes the explanation of the letter-gates of the inner court.
Next, the arrangement of the second courtyard is described: eight Mañjuśrīs are to be placed.
Regarding the method for their placement: in front of the Honored One, facing south, one should paint the Youth Summoner (Ākarṣaṇakumāra).
Next, in the southwest corner, one should paint the Youth Gaṇeśvara (Keśinikumāra).
Next, on the right side of the western direction, paint the youth Jālinīprabha.
Next, in the northwest corner, paint the youth Upakeśinī.
Next, on the rear northern side, paint the youth Jālinīprabha.
Next, in the northeast corner, paint the youth Kṣitigarbha-dhvaja.
Next, on the left side of the east, paint the youth Vimalaprabha.
Next, in the southeast corner, paint the youth Acintyamatī.
In this way, the eight Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta Bodhisattvas from the eight directions all face the central Honored One in a posture of receiving instructions;
each sits upon a lotus flower, individually mounted on a lion.
Each hand should hold its respective insignia and mudrā, drawn according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, within the four corners outside the circular wheel, one should draw the four wrathful vidyārājas.
In the southeast corner, paint Trailokyavijaya-vajra, blue in color and with eight arms.
The two front hands form the mudrā by hooking the right thumb back with the left index finger;
the remaining fists have the thumbs extended upward.
The left hand holds a bow;
the right hand grasps an arrow placed upon the bowstring;
the other left hand holds a pestle.
One hand holds a lasso;
the right hand holds a halberd;
another hand grasps a staff.
He has three faces with fangs bared at the corners of his mouth and sits amidst flames.
In the northwest corner is the four-armed, blue-colored Vidyārāja Aparājita,
who has three faces and fiery hair bristling upward.
The right hand forms a fist with the index finger extended upward;
one hand holds a trident, and one hand performs the *varada* (boon-granting) mudrā.
Holding a staff in one hand, he sits poised upon a lotus.
In the southwest corner is Yamāntaka-vajra, dark blue-black in color,
with six heads, six arms, and six legs, each holding ritual implements.
The upper left hand holds a halberd;
the lower left hand holds a bow;
the lower right hand holds a lasso.
The upper right hand holds a sword;
the next lower hand holds an arrow;
the next lower hand holds a staff.
He rides upon a blue water buffalo as his seat.
In the northeast corner, one should paint Hayagrīva, who has three faces and six arms,
each holding ritual implements and weapons.
The left upper hand holds a lotus;
one hand holds a flask,
and one hand holds a staff at the heart.
He forms two hand mudrās;
his upper right hand holds a battle-axe,
and one [hand] holds a rosary.
Holding a noose with one hand, the Wheel-Turning King sits upon a lotus;
he manifests a great wrathful aspect with an extremely fierce and violent power.
All else follows the original ritual manual.
Next, the outer protection by the sixteen great devas of the third enclosure is described.
In front of the Principal Deity is the Bodhisattva Aṅkuśa (Hook), with his left fist and right hand holding a hook; next to the west is Yama-rāja;
and next to the west is the Lord of Rākṣasas.
One should burn incense in the northeast corner to make offerings to the Bodhisattva;
next, to the north, to the Rākṣasī Queen;
and next, to the north, to Varuṇa.
To the west is the Bodhisattva Sūrya;
next to the north is the Devī Āpa;
and next to the north is the Devaputra Vāyu.
In the northwest corner is the Bodhisattva Puṣpadāna;
next, to the east, is Vāyu-devī;
and next, to the east, is Vaiśravaṇa-rāja.
To the north of the Venerable One is the Bodhisattva Vajrasphoṭā;
next to the east is the consort of Vaiśravaṇa;
and next to the east is the Deva King Īśāna.
The Bodhisattva of the Northeastern Corner’s Lamp Offering;
next to the south, the consort Īśānī;
next to the south, Śakra, King of Devas.
To the left, at the eastern gate, is the Vajraghaṇṭā Bodhisattva;
next to the south is the consort of Śakra;
next to the south is the Fire Deity.
In the southeast corner is the Bodhisattva of Incense Offering;
next to the west is the Goddess of Fire;
and next to the west is Yama.
The above concludes the arrangement of the various deities in the third enclosure.
The four gates and the food offering ritual, as well as the four corners,
follow the same procedures as those for all other mandalas.
The *ratnaja* grass is likewise.
At the four gates, lotus petals are as fine as blue lotuses.
Furthermore, the method for swiftly establishing a mandala to rescue those in distress is explained.
However, one should perform it in a place that is solitary, devoid of people, and free from filth—
whether in a wilderness, a monastery, or an open space—
and thus the rite will immediately possess divine efficacy.
Set aside the upper impure and foul ground and select a pure site.
Compact it firmly so that it is as solid as stone and perfectly level.
Grind white sandalwood into a fine paste to serve as an ointment.
Furthermore, take refined white camphor, frankincense, and other such substances;
soak them to extract a juice like milk,
and use it as an unguent to smear upon the ground.
The first is one cubit, the next two cubits, then three cubits, and four cubits.
It is circular like the lunar disc and divided into four layers;
in the center is the seed-syllable.
Surrounding this is the eight-syllable mantra.
In the second enclosure, one should arrange the eight Mañjuśrī-kumāras.
In the third enclosure, one should arrange the four gatekeepers, the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), and at the four corners, the four great wrathful vidyārājas.
In the fourth courtyard, at the four gates, one should perform offerings of fragrant water, ghee lamps, white flowers, milk porridge, curd-rice, and so forth.
If these cannot be prepared, then simply arrange the Eight Noble Ones in the second courtyard.
Regarding the so-called Four Means of Integration and the Four Vidyārāja Kings:
if one must establish a protected maṇḍala for the sake of a state or a sovereign who is beset by calamities or difficulties.
The altar should be sixteen cubits wide,
or twenty-four cubits for a larger one,
if the five planets have lost their proper courses.
The sun and moon were frequently eclipsed, and comets and meteors appeared repeatedly.
Foreign nations from the four quarters invaded the borders;
the common people were plundered, and high ministers rebelled.
When military expeditions are unfavorable and the people suffer harm while epidemics spread,
one should construct a great mandala.
Within the second enclosure of the mandala, the twelve Great Devas are arrayed outside, according to the method of the Blazing Light (*Cicchengguang*).
Next, the twenty-eight lunar mansions are arrayed in the fourth court;
in the fifth court, the deities of the twelve zodiac signs are placed outside, with the four Vidyārājas arranged as in other rites.
Furthermore, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, men, or women—
Whether they be officials or commoners,
should their persons encounter peril and distress— such as legal troubles, royal displeasure, illness, or any form of terror for which no remedy can be devised—
and should they fear the calamities of swords, staves, or imprisonment;
One should generate a heart of great compassion and perform this recitation at night among the stars,
with either three, five, or seven people.
If one wishes to perform this at the time of need,
one should face north during the night, recite the mantra while calling out the person's name and making aspirations;
by reciting it ten thousand times for each individual, their [karmic obstacles] will be extinguished.
If one intends to perform the practice of recitation, one should be endowed with the eight preparatory methods.
However, when it is appropriate to perform the recitation, one should speak the following verse:
Having bathed and donned clean garments, One adorns the body with fragrant unguents.
Taking refuge and reciting the mantra, with utmost sincerity and reverence,
I pay homage and burn incense to repent of all transgressions; I rejoice in the merit of others, entreat [the Buddhas] to remain,
dedicate the merit, and resolve upon the great vow, giving rise deeply to great compassion.
Thus, having diligently practiced these eight expedient means without forgetfulness,
one should then purify the three karmas and perform, according to the Dharma,
the sequential ritual for the recitation and practice of the Eight-Syllable Secret Dhāraṇī of the Great Holy Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Supreme Majestic Virtue.
I shall now explain according to the dharma-gate of the sequential order of mantras.
First, the practitioner must receive empowerment from an ācārya and obtain the direct oral transmission.
Furthermore, upon re-entering for the empowerment of the vidyādhara-siddhi,
being fully endowed with compassion and practicing unconditional loving-kindness (*nirālamba-maitrī*),
one should recite this while feeling pity for all sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering and distress.
I vow to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from fear and calamity.
Whenever sentient beings encounter urgent distress, one should,
according to the location, prepare an altar by either applying fragrant paste or kneading powdered incense.
If one wishes to practice constant recollection,
one must prepare a pure chamber and establish a *maṇḍala* according to the Dharma, exactly as in the previous ritual.
The practitioner must first give rise to the eight kinds of mind before they may uphold the Dharma.
First, a mind of great compassion; second, a mind free from envy;
third, a mind free from the notion of "mine";
fourth, a mind free from competitiveness.
Fifth, having a mind of equanimity;
sixth, having a mind free from enmity and harm;
seventh, having a mind of compassion.
Eighth, they must be free from greed for profit.
Only such persons may receive the transmission.
Those who possess these qualities are fit to perform the ritual together.
If it were not for this, one would have to perform the rite oneself alone for the ritual to be accomplished; furthermore,
if the prescribed number of recitations has not yet been completed.
One must not suddenly converse with others in the interim to cause an interruption;
otherwise, the efficacy of the rite will be lost.
Before performing the ritual, one should first provide a clear announcement.
If one performs the recitation oneself, it should likewise not be interrupted.
When the practitioner enters the maṇḍala,
they should next perform prostrations with sincere devotion.
Then, with the vajra-palms joined,
one should visualize clearly before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Great Sage Mañjuśrī, the immeasurable bodhisattvas, Vajrapāṇi, and all the worthy sages.
Each person, with their own body, pays homage to the assembly of sages.
The mantra for universally paying homage to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and so forth, is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgata-ghaṭita-vajrapramardana-mañjuśrī-vajranāma-karuṇi. Furthermore, the heart-mantra is as follows:
First, join the vajra-palms; with the ten fingers interlaced externally, let the five wheels [fingers] all touch the ground.
With utmost sincerity and reverence, prostrate and then sit in long-kneeling posture, joining the palms as if holding a lotus.
Visualize the body as a crystal; by adding the syllable HŪṂ to the three places, imagine it becomes the five-pronged vajra.
This is the inner vajra, which constitutes an indestructible essence. Thus, with devotion, perform the invocation.
To all the noble and honored ones who recite these four lines of verse, I bow my head to the Unsurpassed King of Physicians of the Dharma;
O Lord of Compassion, who can save those difficult to save, I now take refuge, pay homage, and entreat you:
I pray only that you will swiftly descend to this site of practice.
Thus, having made the threefold request, one performs the preliminary announcement with palms joined like lotuses;
then, reciting the purification of the three karmas,
one renders the vessel of the body pure and consecrates the five places.
At the forehead, the two shoulders, the heart, and the throat, recite that mantra;
having thus purified the three karmas, form the Buddha-samaya mudrā by joining the palms of wisdom and means like a lotus,
with the two fire-peaks (index fingers) joined and upright.
Bend the two wind-fingers at the upper joints; with the two space-fingers, pinch the roots of the wind-fingers.
Raise the mudrā before the forehead and contemplate all Buddhas clearly and distinctly, as they abide in the midst of empty space.
Recite that mantra as follows: For the Buddha Family Samaya, form the inner-clasped fists of concentration and wisdom;
extend both thumbs side by side and contemplate all Buddhas as if they were standing right before one's eyes.
Recite the mantra while summoning the Honored One with both hands raised together:
"Furthermore, bind the Lotus Family Secret Samaya."
The mudrās are also as before: with the left hand entering and the right extended outward, recite three times and summon three times; settle the right hand and then release it.
Next is the subtle samaya-mudrā of the Vajra family.
First, modify the previous mudrā into the empty wheel (*śūnyacakram*). Insert the right hand into the left and extend it upward in a beckoning gesture;
focus the mind and recollect the Honored One. Recite that mantra as follows:
[The Buddha-family mudrā is placed on the forehead; the Lotus-family mudrā is at the right ear.]
At the left ear of Vajra, scatter [the mudrā] as one would upon the crown of the head.
Next is the Armor Mudrā (Kavaca-mudrā): interlace the *tarjanī* and *madhyamā* fingers with the *karṇikā* and *anāmikā* fingers, inserting them into the palms;
join the tips of the *kaniṣṭhā* and *aṅguṣṭha* fingers together.
The *Jinli* (Power of Advancement) mudrā is curved like a hook;
externally, it is joined with the two *Agni* [fire] fingers behind, while the *Dhyāna* and *Prajñā* fingers stand straight and upright together, resembling a *vajra*.
One should visualize this being added to the five places of the body: the forehead, the right shoulder, and the left.
From the heart, throat, and the aperture at the crown of the head, recite this mantra:
Oṃ kṣaṃ kṣaraḥ jvālottaptavajra vajraprabha vajrasāra vajradhara vajrāyudha vajraśarīra vajrātmaka vajra vajra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Next, explain the *mudrā* of the Vajra Earth Boundary.
In the concentration hand, one should wish for deliverance;
with both hands entering between the precepts and patience, one should clasp and twist them behind the precepts.
Entering between generosity and the precepts, one should wish to twist them into patience and diligence; [this applies to] generosity, wisdom, diligence, and power.
With meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) joined together, perform three rotations and drive it in;
then recite the mantra: Oṃ kili kili vajra vajriṇi bhuvaṃ bhartuṃ bhartuṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Furthermore, explain the seal (*mudrā*) of the Vajra Wall Boundary (*vajraprākārasīmā*).
Using the aforementioned earth-boundary mudrā: extend the *cena* (thumb) and *jñāna* (little finger), join them upright, and rotate them to the right like a wall or courtyard.
While reciting, turn [the mudrā] accordingly, visualizing a vajra-wall. Recite that mantra as follows:
Furthermore, regarding Ākāśagarbha: with the ten perfections as the outer hands, his crossed legs are pressed together like a jewel.
Visualize that a magnificent pavilion is formed, upon which stands a great lotus flower;
contemplate the deity with a concentrated mind.
Dwelling within a jeweled canopy, surrounded on all sides by banners,
pennants, celestial parasols, divine garments, and oceans of fragrant clouds that fill the entirety of space,
he is encircled by his retinue; then one recites this mantra:
Next, bind the chariot seal (*ratha-mudrā*):
Interlace the fingers of the concentration and wisdom hands with palms facing upward, pressing the right over the left;
join the ring and little fingers with the tips of the forefingers and thumbs at the very bottom of the first phalanges, then rotate them forward.
Visualize the formation of a precious chariot; recite that mantra three or seven times.
While maintaining the visualization of welcoming the Honored One, do not release the previous mudrā;
shift the *cena* (middle) and *jñāna* (wisdom) fingers to the tips.
Forming the *añjali* mudrā with the thumbs and ring fingers, visualize the Honored One mounting a carriage;
push it inward three times. Slowly descending to the site of practice, the Honored One abides in the midst of space, awaiting the invitation to enter.
Not transgressing one's original vow, one recites that mantra;
by the power of this mantra and through the application of the mudrā-seal,
one is able to summon the principal deity along with his remaining retinue.
When descending upon the site of practice to bestow blessings upon the practitioner,
and when intending to arrange the ceremonial carriage, one should first purify the path;
holding a censer with both hands, one should recite the secret mantra.
Purify the central path through space; thereafter, invite the Honored Sage, visualizing the incense reaching his palace. Recite this mantra:
"If one performs this sublime rite, the pivot of the void [shall be opened]."
All shall be spontaneously understood and resolved;
likewise, the removal of obstacles and so forth shall be accomplished, as well as the awakening of the Honored One’s retinue and their approach.
Next, first perform the invitation.
After reciting the mantra of the mudrā, summon all the noble deities into the maṇḍala.
Recite the invocation mantra three or seven times to invite them into the ritual arena.
Furthermore, invite Mañjuśrī and Guhyakapāla, the Lord of Vajras;
with the palms joined in the union of wisdom and means, the two fire-fingers (middle fingers) are entwined at the tips of the water-wheel (ring fingers),
and the two wind-fingers (index fingers) are bent so that their tips touch.
